chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Hisham ibn Salim from Al-Hasan ibn Zur'ah from his father said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman according to her ruling (on the dowry). He said: Her ruling does not exceed the dowry of the women of the Family of Muhammad, twelve ounces and a nan, which is the weight of five hundred dirhams of silver. I said: What if you saw that he married her according to his ruling and she accepted? He said: Whatever he ruled regarding something, it is permissible for both of them, whether little or much. He said: I said: How come you did not validate her ruling upon him, but you validated his ruling upon her? He said: Because he made her the arbitrator, so it was not for her to exceed what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) established and married his wives upon, so I returned it to the Sunnah. And because she made him the arbitrator and placed the matter of the dowry in his hands and accepted his ruling in that, so it is upon her to accept his ruling, whether little or much.

key_terms.اثْنَتَيْ عَشْرَةَ أُوقِيَةً: Twelve ounces (a specific weight measure for silver)
key_terms.حُكْمِهَا: Her ruling/decision (referring to her setting the dowry amount)
key_terms.سَنَّ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ: What the Messenger of Allah established/ordained
key_terms.مَهْرَ نِسَاءِ آلِ مُحَمَّدٍ: The dowry of the women of the Family of Muhammad (Prophet's wives)
key_terms.وَزْنُ خَمْسِمِائَةِ دِرْهَمٍ: The weight of five hundred dirhams

ai.seo_question: What is the maximum dowry a wife can set for herself according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s al-Ishtibār clarifies the asymmetry in marital arbitration regarding the dowry (mahr), distinguishing between the wife’s limited authority—capped at the precedent of the Prophet’s wives (12 ounces of silver)—and the husband’s unlimited authority if she consents. The Imam attributes this distinction to the binding nature of the Sunnah on the wife, as she is subject to the Prophet’s established norms, whereas the husband, as the initiator of the arbitration, retains broader discretion. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that consensual agreements (hukm) are valid even if they deviate from standard norms, provided both parties accept the terms.
